claims.claim: In one inner-city geriatric clinic population, 9% had unrecognised BPPV, and those with it were more likely to have had a fall in the previous 3 months.
claims.supporting_passage: We performed a cross-sectional study to determine the prevalence of unrecognized benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) and associated lifestyle sequelae in a public, inner-city geriatric population. Dizziness was found in 61% of patients, whereas balance disorders were found in 77% of patients. Nine percent were found to have unrecognized BPPV. ... Patients with unrecognized BPPV were more likely to have reduced activities of daily living scores, to have sustained a fall in the previous 3 months, and to have depression.
claims.pico_timeframe: Older patients at one US public inner-city geriatric clinic / BPPV not previously recognised / those without it / ADL score, fall in previous 3 months, depression / cross-sectional, year 2000
claims.safe_wording: In one study of patients at a US inner-city clinic for older people, about 9 in 100 turned out to have BPPV that no one had recognised. Those patients were more likely to have had a fall in the previous three months. A snapshot study like this cannot show that the BPPV caused the falls.
claims.qualifications: One clinic, one country, published 2000; not a general prevalence; association only; denominator and sample size not in abstract; do not say 'BPPV causes falls'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Population-level figures are lower (see C14-26-e) because this was a clinic population.

numbers.meaning: share of the clinic sample with unrecognised BPPV; cross-sectional; denominator not in abstract
look-back window for a fall; association only

claims.claim: Posterior canal BPPV is diagnosed with the Dix-Hallpike test and should be treated, or referred for treatment, with a repositioning procedure; the guideline advises against routinely treating BPPV with sedating vestibular suppressants and asks clinicians to assess mobility and falls risk.
claims.supporting_passage: The update group made strong recommendations that clinicians should (1) diagnose posterior semicircular canal BPPV when vertigo associated with torsional, upbeating nystagmus is provoked by the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, performed by bringing the patient from an upright to supine position with the head turned 45° to one side and neck extended 20° with the affected ear down, and (2) treat, or refer to a clinician who can treat, patients with posterior canal BPPV with a canalith repositioning procedure. ... The update group made recommendations against ... (3) routinely treating BPPV with vestibular suppressant medications such as antihistamines and/or benzodiazepines. ... (3) assess patients with BPPV for factors that modify management, including impaired mobility or balance, central nervous system disorders, a lack of home support, and/or increased risk for falling
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 18 and over with suspected BPPV, any setting / guideline recommendations
claims.safe_wording: The 2017 US ENT guideline strongly recommends diagnosing the commonest type of BPPV with the Dix-Hallpike test (head turned 45 degrees, neck extended 20 degrees) and treating it, or referring for treatment, with a repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley. It recommends against routinely treating BPPV with sedating anti-dizziness medicines such as antihistamines or benzodiazepines, and asks clinicians to check mobility, balance and falls risk.
claims.qualifications: US guideline. The named drug classes are antihistamines and benzodiazepines; prochlorperazine is not named in the abstract. The guideline also recommends against routine imaging when BPPV criteria are met.

numbers.meaning: head turn and neck extension in the Dix-Hallpike test as defined in the guideline

claims.claim: The Epley manoeuvre is effective for posterior canal BPPV.
claims.supporting_passage: Complete resolution of vertigo occurred significantly more often in the Epley treatment group when compared to a sham manoeuvre or control (odds ratio (OR) 4.42, 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.62 to 7.44; five studies, 273 participants); the proportion of patients resolving increased from 21% to 56%. ... Some patients were unable to tolerate the manoeuvres because of cervical spine problems. ... There is evidence that the Epley manoeuvre is a safe, effective treatment for posterior canal BPPV, based on the results of 11, mostly small, randomised controlled trials with relatively short follow-up. There is a high recurrence rate of BPPV after treatment (36%).
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 18 to 90 with posterior canal BPPV (positive Dix-Hallpike) / Epley / sham or control / complete resolution of vertigo / short follow-up
claims.safe_wording: In trials, about 56 in 100 people had complete resolution of vertigo after the Epley manoeuvre, compared with about 21 in 100 after a sham manoeuvre or no treatment. BPPV often returns (about 36 in 100 in these trials), and a few people could not tolerate the manoeuvre because of neck problems.
claims.qualifications: Mostly small trials, short follow-up; not specific to frail older people; 'complete resolution' is the stated primary outcome.

numbers.meaning: complete resolution of vertigo, Epley vs sham or control; 5 studies, 273 participants (absolute)
relative effect; do not convert to 'times more likely'
recurrence after treatment

claims.claim: A side-lying version of the test, with head and neck supported, can be used in older people when neck extension is limited.
claims.supporting_passage: It is sometimes difficult to perform the Dix-Hallpike test in elderly persons, due to the limited range of motion when extending the neck. In this study, we used a side-lying test to stimulate the posterior semicircular canal, while the head and neck were fully supported on the examination table. ... A representative population sample of 675 persons completed a questionnaire about dizziness and 571 persons underwent side-lying, static balance and dynamic walking tests. ... BPPV was found in 11% and was significantly more common in women (p<0.01).
claims.pico_timeframe: Representative sample of 75-year-olds in Gothenburg / side-lying test / none / BPPV found, balance tests / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: Because the usual test needs the neck tipped back, which some older people cannot manage, a Swedish study of 75-year-olds used a side-lying version with the head and neck fully supported on the couch. In that study about 11% of those tested were found to have BPPV.
claims.qualifications: Shows the side-lying test was usable in a population sample of 75-year-olds. The abstract does not compare its accuracy with Dix-Hallpike and no guideline in this batch was opened that endorses it, so the post may describe it as a practical option used in research, not as an equal replacement. The 11% denominator is presumably the 571 tested (not stated explicitly).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Accuracy against Dix-Hallpike not established in the abstract read.

numbers.meaning: BPPV found in the tested sample of 75-year-olds (571 tested); definition by side-lying test
people who underwent the clinical tests out of those who completed the questionnaire

claims.claim: BPPV is common in the general population and most affected people do not receive effective treatment.
claims.supporting_passage: The lifetime prevalence of BPPV was 2.4%, the 1 year prevalence was 1.6% and the 1 year incidence was 0.6%. The median duration of an episode was 2 weeks. In 86% of affected individuals, BPPV led to medical consultation, interruption of daily activities or sick leave. In total, only 8% of affected participants received effective treatment. On multivariate analysis, age, migraine, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and stroke were independently associated with BPPV.
claims.pico_timeframe: German adult general population, 2003 survey / BPPV by validated telephone interview / none / prevalence, treatment received / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a German national survey of adults, about 2 in 100 people had had BPPV at some point in life, and only about 8 in 100 of those affected had received effective treatment. Age was one of the factors linked with having it.
claims.qualifications: All adults, not only older people; older figures; the survey identified BPPV by structured interview, not an examination; 'effective treatment' is the authors' term.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Oghalai (9% in a clinic sample) and this survey (2.4% lifetime in adults) measure different things; do not put the two figures side by side as if comparable.

numbers.meaning: lifetime prevalence in German adults (all ages)
share of affected participants who received effective treatment
affected participants whose BPPV led to consultation, interrupted daily activities or sick leave

claims.claim: Prochlorperazine can cause drowsiness and movement side effects in older people (BNF).
claims.location: Not checked (BNF and SmPC not openable in this environment)
claims.safe_wording: Do not name prochlorperazine. Say the guideline advises against routinely treating BPPV with sedating anti-dizziness medicines such as antihistamines or benzodiazepines (C14-26-b).

claims.claim: In a hospice EEG study, all 5 patients recorded when unresponsive showed a brain response to changes in simple tones; none showed the later response that goes with conscious detection of tone changes; 2 of the 5 showed it to changes in a pattern of tones.
claims.supporting_passage: Consistent with control and responsive participants, all (5/5) showed some evidence of either an early fronto-central negativity (MMN), or a later fronto-central positivity (P3a), or both, to tone changes. None of the unresponsive patients showed a centro-parietal positivity (P3b) to the tone changes. One unresponsive patient (20%) showed evidence of a weak late fronto-central positivity (P3a) to pattern changes, and two patients showed stronger centro-parietal positivity (P3b) to pattern changes.
claims.location: Full text, Results (Unresponsive, actively dying, hospice patients)
claims.pico_timeframe: Canadian hospice patients (mostly terminal illness, most on opioids, no delirium or cognitive impairment at entry), 5 recorded when unresponsive (Palliative Performance Scale 10%, 'hours to days' before death) / oddball tone and tone-pattern sequences through headphones / compared with 17 young controls and with the same hospice patients when responsive / event-related potentials (MMN, P3a, P3b) / one session
claims.safe_wording: In a small Canadian hospice study, researchers played tones to 5 people who had stopped responding and were actively dying. All 5 showed a brain response to a change in the tones, which means their hearing system was still reacting. This does not show that they understood what they heard.
claims.qualifications: Use the counts, not 'most': the abstract says 'most unresponsive patients showed evidence of MMN responses', but the Results give 5 of 5 with an MMN or P3a, and the sample is only 5 people. The P3b result in 2 of 5 (to pattern changes only, none to tone changes) is atypical, and the authors say it is 'plausible' these two were aware, not shown; do not report it as evidence of awareness. Time from recording to death is not given per patient; the study defines 'actively dying' as hours to days, so avoid 'hours before death' for these 5.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Abstract wording ('most', 'just hours from end of life') is looser than the Results; the Results govern.

numbers.meaning: unresponsive patients with an MMN or P3a to tone changes
unresponsive patients with a P3b to tone changes
unresponsive patients with a P3b to pattern changes; atypical pattern, interpreted cautiously by the authors
young healthy controls with an MMN or P3a to tone changes

claims.claim: These responses show part of the hearing system was working but do not show understanding or awareness; the authors say the result lends some credence to advice to keep talking to a dying relative.
claims.supporting_passage: It is still unclear how the partial functioning of the auditory change detection system we have reported here relates to normal conscious awareness, in spite of arguments from the existing literature. ... We have presented evidence that at least a few actively dying hospice patients, when they are unable to respond to family or healthcare provider verbal stimuli, nonetheless seem to be hearing and giving neural responses to sequences of simple auditory stimuli. This is consistent with the trope that hearing is one of the last senses to lose function when a person is dying, and lends some credence to the advice that loved ones should keep talking to a dying relative as long as possible.
claims.safe_wording: The study suggests that, in some people, the ear and brain keep reacting to sound close to death. It does not show that the person understood words or knew who was there. The authors say it gives some support to the advice to keep talking to a dying relative.
claims.qualifications: Tones only, not speech or voices of relatives; 'hearing may be one of the last senses to lose function' is the authors' tentative conclusion; the Introduction also says the belief rests mostly on anecdote and near-death-experience reports and that 'the capacity for awareness ... remains unknown'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Small single study with no replication found in this batch.

claims.claim: Study size and limits: 13 patients recruited, 4 excluded for noisy EEG, 9 analysed, 5 recorded when unresponsive; most on opioids; no delirium or cognitive impairment at entry.
claims.supporting_passage: Data were collected initially from 13 participants, residing in a hospice facility in Vancouver, over a time period of more than two years. ... Data from four patients were excluded because of excessive noise in their EEG. The patient analysis to be described is based on nine patients (four female, age 28 to 88 years, mean age 68.2 years). Eight patients were recorded when they were responsive, five when they were unresponsive. ... Note that most patients were receiving various forms of opioids at both recording sessions.
claims.safe_wording: State the size plainly: five people who had stopped responding.
claims.qualifications: Patients were free of delirium and cognitive impairment when enrolled, so the findings may not apply to people with dementia or delirium at the end of life. Ages 28 to 88 apply to the nine analysed patients, not to the five unresponsive recordings alone.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Authors describe their analysis as 'somewhat less conservative' than the original published paradigm.

numbers.meaning: recruited / excluded for EEG noise / analysed / recorded when unresponsive
years, nine analysed patients

claims.claim: Care guidance for the last days of life advises continuing to talk to the dying person.
claims.location: Not found (NICE NG31 and hospice or Marie Curie leaflets not openable; PubMed searches returned nothing usable)
claims.safe_wording: Do not cite guidance. Present speaking to the person, saying who you are, and keeping a hearing aid in while comfortable as a judgement ('We think it is reasonable to ...') supported only by the authors' comment in Blundon 2020; the hearing-aid advice has no source in this batch and must be framed as common-sense practice, not as a finding.
claims.qualifications: Claim dropped as a cited recommendation.

claims.claim: European (EULAR) recommendations say high-dose glucocorticoid should be started immediately in active giant cell arteritis, and the diagnosis should be confirmed by imaging or histology.
claims.supporting_passage: We recommend that a suspected diagnosis of LVV should be confirmed by imaging or histology. High dose glucocorticoid therapy (40-60 mg/day prednisone-equivalent) should be initiated immediately for induction of remission in active giant cell arteritis (GCA) or Takayasu arteritis (TAK).
claims.pico_timeframe: Patients with active GCA or Takayasu arteritis / guideline recommendation
claims.safe_wording: European (EULAR) recommendations say high-dose steroid, 40 to 60 mg a day of prednisolone or equivalent, should start immediately in active giant cell arteritis, and that the diagnosis should be confirmed by scan or biopsy.
claims.qualifications: The abstract does not say in so many words 'start before the test result' or 'same-day fast-track referral'. The practical order (treat first, confirm soon after) is a reasonable reading combined with C14-25-c but should be attributed to the guideline only as 'start immediately'. 'Active GCA' is the guideline's wording; the post should say 'strongly suspected' only when attributing to BSR (see C14-25-b) and BSR cannot yet be cited.

numbers.meaning: prednisone-equivalent starting dose for active GCA

claims.claim: BSR 2020 guideline: strongly suspected GCA treated immediately with high-dose glucocorticoid; specialist review same working day if possible and within 3 working days; new visual loss or double vision seen by an ophthalmologist the same calendar day; higher-dose or intravenous methylprednisolone for visual symptoms; ultrasound and biopsy time windows.
claims.location: Guideline text not opened. Only a WebSearch summary (search extract) was seen: it paraphrased the BSR/NICE 2020 guideline as saying strongly suspected GCA should be treated immediately with high-dose glucocorticoids, with specialist evaluation ideally the same working day and within 3 working days, and new visual loss or double vision seen by an ophthalmologist the same calendar day. The same search found no confirmation of 'ultrasound within one week' or 'biopsy within two weeks' as BSR wording (attributed there to EULAR and the American College of Rheumatology) and no BSR wording on dose for visual symptoms.
claims.pico_timeframe: UK people with suspected GCA / guideline recommendation
claims.safe_wording: Do not attribute any specific statement, time window or visual-symptom dose to the BSR guideline until the guideline text is opened. Alasdair can upload the BSR 2020 PDF (Rheumatology 2020;59:e1-e23) to Drive so the pass can be repeated.
claims.qualifications: Search extract is not enough for an essential claim. The judge's suggested windows (ultrasound about 1 week, biopsy about 2 weeks) are NOT confirmed as BSR wording.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Sources disagree on time windows; the one prospective study opened (C14-25-c) argues for ultrasound as early as possible, preferably within 3 days.

claims.claim: Temporal artery ultrasound becomes less sensitive once glucocorticoid has started, so imaging should be done promptly.
claims.supporting_passage: Before GC exposure, US sensitivity was 94% (95% CI: 83-99), 73% (95% CI: 58-85), and 71% (95% CI: 56-83) when assessing all vessels, TAs, and large vessels (LVs), respectively. At day 3 and 10, the overall US sensitivity was 92% (95% CI: 78-98, P = 0.16) and 83% (95% CI: 69-92, P = 0.10), respectively. At day 10, the TA-US and LV-US sensitivity was 53% (95% CI: 38-68, P < 0.01) and 60% (95% CI: 44-74, P = 0.13), respectively. ... Consistent with the EULAR recommendations, these findings encourage prompt US assessment, preferably within 3 days, to ensure an accurate diagnosis.
claims.pico_timeframe: 48 treatment-naive people with new GCA, Denmark / vascular ultrasound before and at 3 and 10 days after starting glucocorticoid / baseline / ultrasound sensitivity and scores / 10 days
claims.safe_wording: In a small Danish study of 48 people with newly diagnosed giant cell arteritis, ultrasound of the temporal arteries picked up the disease in about 73 in 100 before steroids and about 53 in 100 after 10 days of steroids. The authors advise ultrasound as soon as possible after starting treatment, preferably within 3 days. Treatment should not wait for the scan.
claims.qualifications: Small single-centre study; the last sentence ('treatment should not wait') comes from the EULAR statement in C14-25-a, not from this study. Whole-body ultrasound sensitivity fell less (94% to 83%, not clearly different). Temporal-artery drop was clear (P<0.01). The abstract does not name the reference standard. Cannot be used to say that ultrasound or biopsy remain informative for 1 or 2 weeks.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Older (1984) data in a geriatric review in Alasdair's Drive (Frearson 2003, quoting Allison) reported biopsy positivity falling from 82% before steroids to 60% at one week and 10% at two weeks; newer sources suggest biopsy stays useful longer. Not used because it is a secondary and old figure.

numbers.meaning: temporal-artery ultrasound sensitivity before steroids vs day 10; 48 patients; 95% CI 58-85 and 38-68
all-vessel ultrasound sensitivity before steroids vs day 10; difference not clearly significant (P=0.10)
authors' suggested latest time to ultrasound

claims.claim: Sight loss in giant cell arteritis can be permanent, and can still occur in a small number of people after treatment has started.
claims.supporting_passage: Permanent visual loss is the main short-term complication. [Castaneda 2022, Abstract] ... Eleven out of 502 patients (2.2%) experienced a new PVL including 6 occurrences during the initial therapeutic phase and 5 during the tapering phase. [Curumthaullee 2022, Abstract] ... Headache and visual disturbances including loss of vision are characteristic of GCA. Constitutional symptoms and elevated inflammatory markers (>90%) are common in both diseases. [Buttgereit 2016, Abstract]
claims.pico_timeframe: Giant cell arteritis, mainly aged 50+ / permanent visual loss as complication
claims.safe_wording: Giant cell arteritis can cause permanent sight loss, which is why it is treated as an emergency. Headache and sight problems are typical features, and tiredness, weight loss and other whole-body symptoms are also common.
claims.qualifications: No opened source gives a proportion who lose sight permanently without treatment, and none says visual loss is 'usually' permanent; do not use 'usually'. Curumthaullee: new permanent sight loss after starting steroid was rare (2.2%, single French centre, 1976 to 2020), so 'treatment prevents all sight loss' must not be implied. 'Constitutional symptoms ... common' is from a statement that covers both PMR and GCA.

numbers.meaning: patients with new permanent visual loss after glucocorticoid start; retrospective single-centre inception cohort

claims.claim: Older people with giant cell arteritis may present with unusual features; people with only unusual features are treated later.
claims.supporting_passage: Of 21,828 screened records, 429 studies corresponding to 746 individuals (median [IQR] age 72 [IQR, 66-78] years, 63% female) with at least one atypical feature of GCA were included. Eighty-two percent had both atypical and at least one concurrent typical giant cell arteritis feature, whereas 18% of patients with atypical signs and symptoms only presented with atypical features. ... Patients with atypical features only experienced greater delay in treatment initiation (p < 0.001). The most commonly reported atypical signs/symptoms were vertigo (11.9%), scalp necrosis/ulceration (7.9%), and dry cough (5.8%).
claims.pico_timeframe: 746 people (median age 72) with biopsy-proven GCA and at least one atypical feature, from case reports and series / atypical-only vs atypical plus typical features / time to treatment / systematic review
claims.safe_wording: A review of published cases of giant cell arteritis found that some people, median age 72, have only unusual features such as vertigo, scalp ulceration or a dry cough, and these people had longer delays before treatment started. The authors advise checking inflammatory markers early in unexplained illness.
claims.qualifications: Built from case reports, so it shows that atypical presentations exist and are linked with delay, not how common they are. The named atypical features do not include weight loss or jaw ache (jaw claudication is a typical feature), so the post should not list those as 'atypical' on this source.

numbers.meaning: of the 746 cases had only atypical features (selected case-report population, not a prevalence)
years, IQR 66-78

claims.claim: Intravenous glucocorticoid is used for people with ischaemic (including visual) complications.
claims.supporting_passage: Glucocorticoids (oral, or intravenous in cases with ischaemic complications) remain the first line treatment for GCA.
claims.safe_wording: A Swedish national guideline says steroids may be given intravenously when there are ischaemic complications, such as sight loss. The UK guideline wording on dose for visual symptoms has not been checked.
claims.qualifications: Swedish guideline, not BSR; does not give a dose or say that visual symptoms alone trigger intravenous treatment. Do not describe it as the UK recommendation.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: BSR dosing for visual symptoms not verified (C14-25-b).

claims.claim: Losing both sight and hearing is not rare in older people, and each loss makes it harder to follow speech.
claims.supporting_passage: In combination dual sensory loss occurs. Dual sensory loss is becoming a more common condition seen by clinicians and previous research has shown that 6% of non-institutionalized older adults had a dual sensory impairment, whilst 70% of severely vision-impaired older adults also demonstrated a significant hearing loss. Decreased vision and/or hearing acuity interferes with reception of the spoken message and hence people with sensory loss frequently experience communication breakdown. [Heine and Browning 2002] ... Half of the participants had normal hearing and vision, 38% impaired hearing, 5% impaired vision, and 7% had dual-sensory impairment. [Dupuis 2015, 301 adults, mean age 71]
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults / narrative review and one convenience sample
claims.safe_wording: Losing both sight and hearing is not rare in later life, and poorer sight or poorer hearing each make speech harder to follow. Do not give a percentage.
claims.qualifications: Heine and Browning figures are quoted from earlier research (2002). Dupuis 2015 is a single sample of 301 community adults (mean age 71), so 7% is not a population prevalence (the judge asked for a population estimate or omission). No UK population estimate was found in an opened source. The step 'lip-reading needs sight' is common-sense reasoning not stated in the abstracts.

claims.claim: In England, the 2014 Care Act deafblind policy guidance requires councils to identify and keep a record of deafblind people and to arrange an assessment by a specifically trained person.
claims.location: Not opened (GOV.UK blocked, HTTP 403 via proxy). Search extract only; it summarised the guidance as requiring councils to contact and keep a record of deafblind people and to have assessments done by someone with specific deafblind expertise; published 18 December 2014; issued under section 78 of the Care Act 2014 for adults.
claims.safe_wording: Cannot be stated as fact in a post yet. If the guidance PDF is placed in Drive or opened by another route, a possible wording is: 'In England, government guidance under the Care Act says councils should identify deafblind people and arrange an assessment by a suitably trained person.' Current-version status also needs checking.
claims.qualifications: Search extract is not enough for an essential claim; one of the extracts was a Sense (charity) summary, not the primary document.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Whether the 2014 version is still current is unconfirmed.

claims.claim: Scotland's See Hear framework covers services for people with sensory impairment, including dual sensory loss.
claims.location: Not searched (reserve candidate; official web pages cannot be opened)
claims.qualifications: Not attempted because the statutory claim in C14-23-b already prevents 'ready'.

candidates.reason: Core claims are supported by sources read this pass: Dix-Hallpike diagnosis, repositioning treatment and advice against routine sedating suppressants (AAO-HNS 2017 abstract); Epley 56 vs 21 in 100 resolved (Cochrane abstract); 9% unrecognised BPPV in a clinic sample with an association with a recent fall (Oghalai abstract); and a side-lying test used in a population sample of 75-year-olds because neck extension is difficult (Kollen 2012 abstract). The prochlorperazine/BNF claim was not found and is dropped.
candidates.revised_angle: Keep the angle, with these wording limits: present 9% as one US clinic sample and the fall link as association only; say the guideline advises against routinely treating BPPV with antihistamines or benzodiazepines (do not name prochlorperazine); describe the side-lying test as a practical option used in a 75-year-old population study, not as a proven equal of Dix-Hallpike; mention that BPPV recurs in about a third and that a few people cannot tolerate the manoeuvres because of neck problems.

candidates.reason: Full text of Blundon 2020 was opened and the numbers checked: 5 people recorded when unresponsive; 5 of 5 had an MMN or P3a to tone changes; none had a P3b to tone changes; 2 of 5 had a P3b to pattern changes. The authors state that the link to awareness is unclear, so the post must not imply understanding. The NICE/last-days guidance claim could not be sourced and is dropped; speaking to the person is presented as the authors' suggestion and as judgement.

The BSR 2020 guideline text could not be opened by any route (no abstract or PMC copy in PubMed; Scite at its monthly limit; Undermind could not retrieve the PDF; not in Drive; official web pages blocked), so the claims the angle depends on (BSR wording, ultrasound/biopsy time windows, dose for visual symptoms, 'visual loss usually permanent') cannot be supported. What is supported: EULAR 2018 recommendation to start high-dose glucocorticoid immediately in active GCA with confirmation by imaging or histology; a prospective study showing temporal-artery ultrasound sensitivity falling by day 10 of steroids; permanent sight loss as the main short-term complication; and a systematic review linking atypical-only presentations (median age 72) with treatment delay.
candidates.revised_angle: Teach the order and the older-person trap using the supported sources: in suspected GCA, EULAR advises starting high-dose steroid immediately and confirming by scan or biopsy; do not wait for the test; arrange ultrasound or biopsy promptly because temporal-artery ultrasound picks up less after about 10 days of steroids (73 to 53 in 100 in a 48-patient study); sight loss can be permanent; unusual or vague presentations in older people (median age 72 in the review) are linked with later treatment. Attribute to EULAR, not BSR. Do not give BSR time windows, a dose for visual symptoms, or 'usually permanent'. To restore the BSR-based version, Alasdair can upload the BSR 2020 guideline PDF to Drive and this pass can be repeated.

candidates.reason: Reserve and fallback for C14-18. The key policy claim (England's deafblind guidance requires councils to identify people and arrange a specialist assessment) rests on a search extract only because GOV.UK cannot be opened, and the See Hear framework was not checked. The dual-loss prevalence figure is a 301-person convenience sample (Dupuis 2015) and the other figure is a 2002 secondary quote. Only the general point that each sense loss makes speech harder to follow is partly supported.
candidates.revised_angle: As a fallback only if the deafblind guidance PDF is placed in Drive or opened by another route. Otherwise, narrow to the practical point without statutory claims or percentages: when assessing an older person's hearing, ask about sight, and the reverse, because each loss makes speech harder to follow; people with both may need assessment that considers both. Do not state what councils must do.
